summary: A 1975 working paper on how to keep duplicated copies of a database consistent across a network. It discusses the general problem, then gives a detailed solution for one kind of duplicate database. The ideas were used for the TIP user identification database.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 677 describes how independent computers can keep copies of a database in step despite delays and communication failures. It uses timestamps to choose updates and keeps deletion records long enough to handle late messages.

questions: how do duplicate databases stay consistent
subtitle: A working design for keeping database copies consistent across unreliable network links.

tldr.problem: Separate computers may keep copies of the same database, but network delays and failures mean those copies cannot always match immediately.
tldr.mechanism: Each update carries a timestamp and the identity of the database process that made it. Copies keep the later update, and retain deletion marks until old updates can no longer arrive.
tldr.outcome: The paper describes a way for copies to converge after updates stop and communication resumes. Its ideas were used for the TIP user identification database.

today: RFC 677 is a working paper describing techniques for duplicated databases. It says its concepts were used in designing the TIP user identification database.

sections.title: Why Keep Duplicate Databases
sections.content:
The paper considers databases copied across several independent database management processes (DBMPs). Copies can improve data access reliability and speed, but the processes communicate over network paths that can fail or be interrupted.

Because updates take time to travel, the copies cannot be identical at every moment. The stated goal is that after updates stop and the processes have enough time to communicate, each entry will have the same existence and value in every copy.
sections.plainLanguage: Several computers can keep copies so data remains available and close to users. A copy may be temporarily behind while updates travel.

sections.title: Ordering Updates with Timestamps
sections.content:
Each modification receives a timestamp paired with the identifier of the DBMP that originated it. Timestamps are ordered first by time and, when times match, by the ordered DBMP identifiers. This gives every DBMP the same way to decide which assignment to keep when updates arrive in different orders.

The paper notes a limitation: clocks at different sites may disagree. If they are sufficiently out of synchrony, a later real-world assignment can receive an earlier timestamp and lose.
sections.plainLanguage: Every change carries its time and the identity of the computer that made it. All copies compare those marks and keep the update ranked later.

sections.title: Creation, Deletion, and Cleanup
sections.content:
An entry records its selector, value, deletion flag, creation timestamp, and latest modification timestamp. Keeping the creation time lets a DBMP distinguish an old assignment from an assignment to a newly created entry with the same selector.

A deleted entry is marked rather than immediately erased. The paper describes exchanging timestamp summaries so a DBMP can determine when all other DBMPs have received the deletion and the entry can safely be removed.
sections.plainLanguage: A deletion leaves a marked record behind, so an old update cannot accidentally restore the entry. The copies can remove that record after they know the deletion has reached the others.
